highlights: On 6 May the U.S.-Soviet Joint Commission adjourned sine die after the Soviets sought to exclude parties that had criticized trusteeship; General Shtikov left for North Korea on 8 May.
The FY 1946-47 national budget was approved: expenditure ¥11,800,212,360 against income ¥8,013,393,996, leaving a deficit of about ¥3.79 billion.
Cholera broke out at Pusan at the end of May (24 deaths in 74 cases by the 31st); the city was quarantined and its 400,000 residents were inoculated.
Controlled staple foods fell to 30,000 metric tons on 1 May and the daily ration was cut to 150 grams; a 1946 rice crop 23 percent below 1945's is forecast.
By 2 June, 736,527 Japanese had been repatriated and 973,923 Koreans had returned to South Korea; refugees crossing the 38th parallel rose to 8,314 in the week ending 18 May.
Ordinances 70-90 were promulgated, including the ban on sale of females (No. 70), abolition of the Offices of Planning (No. 81) and Provincial Affairs (No. 74), and the railway merger (No. 75).
A rightist anti-trusteeship rally of about 50,000 in Seoul on 12 May ended in an unauthorized parade and attacks on Communist headquarters and three left-wing newspapers.
Counterfeiters who circulated ¥9,000,000 in bogus notes were arrested; their equipment was found in the building housing Korean Communist Party headquarters.

summary: Summation No. 8 covers May 1946 in South Korea under USAMGIK, with Lt. Gen. Hodge commanding USAFIK and Maj. Gen. Archer Lerch as Military Governor. It opens with a three-section digest (Part I) and then gives fuller Political, Economic and Social parts. The central political event is the 6 May adjournment sine die of the U.S.-Soviet Joint Commission over whether anti-trusteeship groups could be consulted. The report prints the American statements in full and surveys Korean press and public reaction. Other developments include the abolition of the Offices of Planning and Provincial Affairs, decentralized property custody, railway consolidation, and the FY 1946-47 budget (¥11.8 billion expenditure against ¥8.0 billion income). The economic sections stress the worsening rice shortage, summer grain collection and barter plans, and a late-May cholera outbreak at Pusan. Other topics are repatriation and the refugee flow across the 38th parallel, police reform and public-order incidents, and a long background study of Korean postal, savings and insurance systems. Historians will find ordinance lists, judicial appointments, statistical tables and press summaries useful.
